Q: Lazy IO and concurrency in Haskell A:

You shouldn't use lazy I/O, but if you're going to ignore that advice, you should at least use it in a way that makes sense. For your makeA operation here, it doesn't make sense to defer the whole operation until later. Assuming the value is actually needed at some point, you don't save any time by waiting for it later instead of waiting for it now, and if you then, on top of that, force the user of your lazy I/O operations to explicitly run them in parallel (whether via par or your own invented epar) at the point of use, you've made what should be a more convenient interface into an outright burden.

If you want to make effective use of lazy I/O here, you want your makeA to launch the expensive operation in the background and then defer only the delay of waiting on the response for the future. In other words, you want something like this:

makeA = do
  result <- newEmptyMVar
  _ <- forkIO $ do
    putStrLn "Querying a"
    threadDelay 1_000_000
    putStrLn "Got a"
    putMVar result 1
  unsafeInterleaveIO $ readMVar result

With makeB defined the same way, the operations are automatically interleaved without having to use par. And, lazy I/O is being used the way it was intended -- giving the illusion of immediately completing a slow I/O operation and returning its result as a pure value.

Here's a full example:

import Control.Concurrent
import System.IO.Unsafe

deferred ::  IO a -> IO a
deferred act = do
  result <- newEmptyMVar
  _ <- forkIO $ act >>= putMVar result
  unsafeInterleaveIO $ readMVar result

makeA, makeB :: IO Int
makeA = deferred $ do
  putStrLn "Querying a"
  threadDelay 1_000_000
  putStrLn "Got a"
  return 1

makeB = deferred $ do
  putStrLn "Querying b"
  threadDelay 1_000_000
  putStrLn "Got b"
  return 2

f :: Int -> Int -> Int
f a b = a + b

main :: IO ()
main = do
    a <- makeA
    b <- makeB
    let c = f a b
    print c

When run under GHCi, it prints something like:

λ> main
QuQeureyriynign ga 
b
<one second pause>
Got Gao
t b
3

with the interleaved text indicating that the operations are running in parallel, without needing any explicit par or anything.

Q: Perl dynamically generated multidimentional associative array A:

Assigning to the hash the way you have should work fine. You are declaring your variables improperly. Your associative array is called a hash in Perl, and is prefixed with a % sigil, so you should write my %data before the while loop. Inside the loop, the my operator needs parens to apply to a list, so it should be my ($ID, $COUNT);.

This minimal example works properly:

use warnings;  # place these lines at the top of all of your programs
use strict;    # they will catch many errors for you

my %data;  # hash variable
while (<DATA>) {
    chomp;
    my ($id, $count) = split /,/;  # simplify the split

    $data{$id}{count} = $count;    # build your hash
}

print "got: $data{des313}{count}\n";  # prints "got: 3"

__DATA__
des313,3

Q: Does IEEE754 really mandate (nan == nan) to be false? A:

== is not a test of whether two numbers are equal or unequal or whether two floating-point operands are identical or not. Such a test would not yield a Boolean results—it would yield one of two results, equal or unequal, but it would not yield one of the Boolean results, true or false.

== is a test of whether its two operands are equal numbers. If both operands are a number, and the operands are equal, then it yields the Boolean result of true, correctly indicating the operands are two equal numbers. If either operand is not a number, or they are both numbers but are not equal, then it yields the Boolean result of false, correctly indicating the operands are not two equal numbers. (There is an exception to this: If either operation is a signaling NaN, then the operation signals a floating-point exception.)

Yes, IEEE 754-2019 requires that the “compareQuietEqual” operation behave this way. It does not require that the == operator map to this operation.

IEEE 754-2019 also requires there be a “compareSignalingEqual” operation that signals when either operand is a NaN. For example, C provides that operation, more or less, with the iseqsig macro.

[Question] If a language implemented the IEEE predicates as named functions, but kept a richer ternary logic for relational operators, could it still claim compliance?

The standard has no jurisdiction in which operators are used for which operations in an implementation and has no prohibitions on implementations providing operations beyond what it requires or describes. So, if an implementation provided the operations that IEEE-754 requires as named functions or by other means, then it would conform to the standard, and providing additional operations via “relational operators” would not break that conformance.

Q: Postgresql server closed the connection unexpectedly A:

This is not a PostgreSQL query issue. The server log says the client connection was forcibly closed, while the client reports ECONNRESET.

Since it only happens on one Linux machine and only with larger responses, check that client’s network path, especially MTU, VPN, firewall, router or network driver.

Try lowering the MTU temporarily:

sudo ip link set dev eth0 mtu 1400

Replace eth0 with the correct interface from:

ip link

Also test the same machine on another network. If the connection drops only after being idle for some time, configure PostgreSQL TCP keepalives such as tcp_keepalives_idle.
